title: When Customs Differ
short: Customs vary by region, country and family; as a guest, follow your host's way, and never mock or correct another family's customs.
trouble: Learners call a different custom "wrong," such as eating with the fork in the left hand or taking shoes off at the door. Different is not rude; correcting others is.

blocks.html: Since etiquette is a code that changes with time and place, it follows that different families, regions and countries use different codes. This course teaches present-day American custom as its base, with notes where people do things differently. Those notes matter as much as the rules.
Customs vary by region, country and family. As a guest, follow your host's way. Never mock or correct another family's customs: different is not rude, but correcting others is.

The purpose of every custom is to put people at ease. A host's customs are how that home makes people comfortable, so following them honors the host. Telling someone their way is "wrong" does the opposite: it makes them feel judged in their own home or culture. The guest who adapts gracefully is the one practicing good manners.

head: Custom
Some ways people do it
rows: Many homes ask guests to take shoes off; others keep them on. Follow the host, and if unsure, ask.
American style switches the fork to the right hand; Continental style keeps it in the left. Both are correct.
A handshake, a bow, a nod, a cheek kiss, a hand on the heart.
Some families say a blessing or a few words first; some begin when the host lifts a fork.
Mr. or Ms. with a last name, "Miss Ana," first names, or sir and ma'am.
blocks.cap: A few customs that vary. None of these ways is rude.

blocks.title: A different custom at a friend's table
blocks.q: At Omar's family dinner, everyone waits while his grandfather says a few words before eating. Leo's family never does this. What should Leo do?
steps: Notice the custom and follow the host's lead.
Wait quietly with hands in his lap until the family begins.
He doesn't need to join words he doesn't share; waiting respectfully is enough.
blocks.a: Wait quietly and begin when the family does.

blocks.title: A comment that goes wrong
blocks.q: Ruby sees a guest eating with the fork in her left hand, tines down, and says, "You're holding your fork wrong." Was Ruby right?
steps: Check the facts: the guest is using the Continental style, which is correct.
Even if it were a slip, correcting a guest at the table embarrasses her.
Ruby's comment is the rude part, not the guest's fork.
blocks.a: No. Different is not wrong, and correcting others is the real breach.

blocks.html: Calling a different custom "wrong," such as eating with the fork in the left hand or taking shoes off at the door. Different is not rude; correcting others is. Quick check: does this custom cause anyone harm or discomfort? If not, it is simply another way.
Customs differ: when you visit a home or a country with customs you don't know, watch, ask quietly, and follow along. People are almost always glad you asked.
